source: Slusarz & Sun (2001) The interaction of explicit and implicit learning: an integrated model (CogSci 23)
finding: CLARION (explicit rules on top, neural net below) was fitted to human process-control data of Stanley et al. (1989). Verbalising during practice and giving explicit instructions both raised human scores, and the model reproduced both.
numbers: Human data: 12 to 31 subjects per group, 200 trials. Verbalisation effect: original vs control F(1,73)=5.20, p<.05. Memory-training and simple-rule groups also beat control. Model matched with t tests, p<.01.
limits: Fit is qualitative (ordering of groups). Parameters (rule deletion threshold, level weights) were set per task by hand. Human subject numbers small.
agent_relevance: Explicit instruction on top of an implicit learner helps, as a scaffold on an LLM may. Strongest support is for a rule layer that is cheap to add.

source: Slusarz & Sun (2001) The interaction of explicit and implicit learning: an integrated model (CogSci 23)
finding: Berry and Broadbent (1988) data: explicit search help hurt when the task was non-salient (hard to see the rule) and helped when salient. Explicit instructions helped in all conditions. The model reproduced this.
numbers: Set 2: salient experimental group > salient control (p<.01); non-salient experimental < non-salient control (p<.05). Set 3: both instructed groups > control (p<.01). Model needed rule-deletion threshold raised from 0.1 to 0.5 and level weights set 0.5/0.5 to capture the search effect.
limits: Boundary condition: synergy is not universal. Parameters changed by hand between phases, so this is a fit not a prediction.
agent_relevance: Forcing explicit hypothesis search can lower accuracy when the pattern is not salient. A schema should not force rule-stating on every task.

source: Slusarz & Sun (2001) The interaction of explicit and implicit learning: an integrated model (CogSci 23)
finding: Slusarz and Sun credit Sun and Peterson (1998) for the source of synergy between levels: discrete rules vs continuous values, one-shot rule learning vs gradual Q-value learning, and the bottom-up rule-extraction criterion.
numbers: Three stated factors. No new effect size. Claim: human synergy is 'very likely' from the same factors.
limits: Mechanistic inference from model fit, not a test with a rival model. Authors admit implicit learning is 'controversial'.
agent_relevance: Suggests the gain comes from two learners with different error profiles, not from the rule layer alone. An LLM plus a separate checker has the same shape.

source: Sun (2005) From Hybrid Systems to Hybrid Cognitive Architectures (NeSy05 slides)
finding: CLARION fit to the letter-counting task of Rabinowitz and Goldberg (1995) with four groups: control, original, memory training, simple rule. The full model (independent rule learning plus implicit net) fit better than ablated versions.
numbers: Human means, sugar/person tasks: control 1.97/2.85, original 2.57/3.75, memory training 4.63/5.33, simple rule 4.00/5.91. Mean squared error of the full model 0.113 total. Ablation IDN+RER MSE 1.231; IDN+IRL MSE 0.384. Second run: IDN+RER 1.016, IDN+IRL 0.285.
limits: Slides, not the paper. Slide headings mix up two tasks, so treat labels with care. Fit to group means only. No held-out test.
agent_relevance: Ablation shows the rule-extraction pathway alone does not explain human gains; the interplay does. Weak support but a clean ablation design to copy.

source: Sun (2005) From Hybrid Systems to Hybrid Cognitive Architectures (NeSy05 slides)
finding: List of tasks CLARION has been fitted to: process control, serial reaction time, artificial grammar learning, alphabetic arithmetic, categorical inference, discovery tasks, Tower of Hanoi, minefield navigation, metacognitive monitoring.
numbers: About 11 tasks, all fitted mainly with bottom-up learning. No count of failed fits is reported.
limits: Only successes are listed. No failed or rival-model comparisons in the slides.
agent_relevance: Breadth is claimed but selection bias is possible. Do not treat CLARION as a validated predictor.

source: Sun (2025) Enhancing Computational Cognitive Architectures with LLMs: A Case Study
finding: Proposes replacing CLARION's small backprop implicit level with an LLM and keeping the explicit rule level. The LLM plays intuition and instinct; explicit rules can veto, verify or explain.
numbers: No measured results. It is a position paper with examples. Cites Dasgupta 2022 and Trott 2023 as evidence that LLMs show human-like content effects and false-belief performance.
limits: Not peer reviewed, no benchmark. The claim that LLM equals human intuition is argued, not tested. Author admits LLM symbolic skills are limited.
agent_relevance: Closest statement of our design (LLM as implicit layer, schema as explicit layer). But no evidence yet that it beats a plain LLM.

source: Sun (2025) Enhancing Computational Cognitive Architectures with LLMs: A Case Study
finding: Says CLARION's own shortcomings are limited implicit knowledge, limited implicit-explicit interaction, and no language. Lists missing interaction types: veto (Libet), default-intervention (Evans), and an inner dialogue between explicit and implicit (Helie and Sun 2010).
numbers: Four-step creative loop: explicit prep, implicit work, explicit validate, send back if wrong. No effect sizes.
limits: Helie and Sun (2010) is a model fit, not an intervention study.
agent_relevance: The four-step loop maps to generate, verify, return-with-feedback. A candidate operator pattern.

source: Sun (2024) Can a cognitive architecture fundamentally enhance LLMs? Or vice versa?
finding: Argues LLMs are mostly implicit processing and need an explicit symbolic partner. One example: an insight puzzle failed until the prompt added an explicit hint.
numbers: Single anecdote: plant four trees all equidistant in 3D failed; adding 'This task has a simple solution. Please present its solution with less than 30 words' gave the tetrahedron answer. N=1 prompt, no repeats.
limits: Anecdote only. Prompt hint leaks that the answer is short, so it may be a length effect.
agent_relevance: Shows how weak the evidence is. Needs a controlled test before we rely on it.

source: Sun (2024) Can a cognitive architecture fundamentally enhance LLMs? Or vice versa?
finding: Cites mixed results on LLM reasoning (Dasgupta; Saparov and He; Trott; Zhang) and Bubeck et al. on missing planning, working memory and backtracking.
numbers: No new numbers.
limits: Secondary citations only.
agent_relevance: Backs a scaffold that adds planning and backtracking from outside.

source: Sun (2025), description of bottom-up and top-down learning in CLARION
finding: Bottom-up learning extracts explicit rules from successful implicit actions using information gain. Top-down learning uses explicit rules to give reinforcement to the implicit net. Two levels are combined by stochastic selection weighted by each level's recent performance.
numbers: No numbers in this paper. Original studies: Sun, Merrill and Peterson (2001); Sun et al. (2005).
limits: Description of an algorithm, not a test of it.
agent_relevance: Performance-weighted choice between a fast answer and a rule-based answer is a concrete arbitration rule.

source: Lin et al. (2023) SwiftSage: a generative agent with fast and slow thinking for complex interactive tasks
finding: A fast small module (fine-tuned Flan-T5) plus a slow GPT-4 planner, switched by a heuristic, beat ReAct, Reflexion and SayCan on ScienceWorld.
numbers: ScienceWorld, 30 task types. GPT-4 overall score: SwiftSage 84.7, Reflexion 45.3, ReAct 36.4, SayCan 33.8. Oracle 100. By length: short 92.2, medium 77.8, long 83.0 for SwiftSage.
limits: Small benchmark with fixed procedural tasks. Fast module was trained on oracle trajectories, so it carries task-specific training, not a pure scaffold.
agent_relevance: Strongest LLM evidence for hybrid fast/slow. Part of the gain comes from training the fast module, which we cannot do.

source: Lin et al. (2023) SwiftSage: a generative agent with fast and slow thinking for complex interactive tasks
finding: Robustness to a weaker LLM: with GPT-3.5-turbo baselines fell sharply but SwiftSage held up.
numbers: GPT-3.5: SwiftSage 62.22, SayCan 25.22, Reflexion 23.40, ReAct 19.76 (ReAct was 36.43 with GPT-4). First column of Table 3 reads 49.22 overall, likely the fast module alone.
limits: Column labelling in the extracted table is not certain. Single run per setting.
agent_relevance: The fast module carries much of the score when the LLM is weak. A scaffold may help weak models most.

source: Lin et al. (2023) SwiftSage: a generative agent with fast and slow thinking for complex interactive tasks
finding: Cost: SwiftSage needs fewer tokens per action and gets more score per action than ReAct and Reflexion. Switching rules are hand written heuristics.
numbers: Table 4 reports tokens per action and score per action. A small ablation says adding grounding questions Q1-Q3 gave about 2 points on short tasks.
limits: Heuristic switch not tuned or compared against alternatives in detail. Only ScienceWorld.
agent_relevance: Switching between modes can save tokens. But the arbitration rule is the weak part.

source: Christakopoulou et al. (2024) Agents thinking fast and slow: a Talker-Reasoner architecture
finding: A fast Talker answers using the last stored belief while a slow Reasoner updates beliefs and plans in the background. Qualitative only: a sleep coaching agent.
numbers: No quantitative results. Two failure modes named: 'Intuitive Talker' works when an old belief is enough; 'Snap judgement Talker' fails on multi-step plans or tool calls when the Reasoner has not finished.
limits: No benchmark, no human evaluation. Single domain.
agent_relevance: Gives a boundary condition: asynchronous fast answers are unsafe when the task needs the slow result. Add a wait gate.

source: Yu et al. (2024) Distilling System 2 into System 1
finding: Fine-tuning Llama-2-70B-chat on its own System 2 outputs (without the intermediate reasoning) made it fast and sometimes as good, but not for chain of thought.
numbers: Rephrase and Respond, last letter: System 1 30.0%, 2-step RaR 39.5%, distilled 98.0%. Coin flip: System 1 56.1%, 2-step RaR 77.2%, distilled 75.69%. S2A TriviaQA: System 1 51.6%, S2A 76.0%, distilled 81.3% (tokens 165 vs 56).
limits: Needs training, so not usable by a pure scaffold. Distillation worked only where System 2 output was consistent.
agent_relevance: Where distillation fails, System 2 steps cannot be dropped; the explicit layer stays needed.

source: Yu et al. (2024) Distilling System 2 into System 1
finding: Failure: distilling chain of thought on GSM8k did not work. This is the main boundary condition.
numbers: GSM8k: System 1 9.40%, System 2 (CoT zero-shot) 52.77%, distilled CoT 7.13%. 7461 unlabeled training questions.
limits: Authors say it fails; no fix tested. One model.
agent_relevance: Math reasoning needs the explicit steps. Do not expect an implicit shortcut to replace them.

source: Yu et al. (2024) Distilling System 2 into System 1
finding: Branch-Solve-Merge distillation raised agreement on OASST2 above the teacher, with a consistency filter.
numbers: OASST2: distilled BSM 58.4% vs System 1 44.7% and BSM 48.7%; tokens 4 vs 603.7. Removing the self-consistency filter (USC) lowered TriviaQA 81.3 to 78.6.
limits: Agreement with GPT-4 labels, not truth. Unsupervised filter matters.
agent_relevance: Self-consistency as a filter is a cheap check that raises quality.

source: Romero et al. (2023) Synergistic integration of LLMs and cognitive architectures for robust AI: an exploratory analysis
finding: Proposes four ways to join an LLM with a cognitive architecture: modular, agency, neuro-symbolic, and CLARION-style. Shows ChatGPT writing ACT-R productions and symbolic facts.
numbers: No benchmark numbers. Examples only, with ChatGPT and GPT-4 prompts.
limits: Exploratory analysis. No ablation or test against a plain LLM.
agent_relevance: Confirms that there is no measured gain yet for architecture plus LLM beyond SwiftSage-type tests.

source: Kambhampati et al. (2024) LLMs can't plan, but can help planning in LLM-Modulo frameworks
finding: A generator LLM plus external verifiers that send back critiques. Alone, LLM plans rarely work. With a verifier loop they improve a lot.
numbers: Autonomous GPT-4: about 12% of plans executable and goal reaching. With VAL verifier: Blocks World 82% within 15 rounds, Logistics 70%, obfuscated Mystery BW about 10%. TravelPlanner GPT-3.5 best prompt strategies 0.7%.
limits: The verifier is a sound external model, not another LLM. Mystery BW shows the loop fails if the generator cannot produce candidates.
agent_relevance: Hybrid works when the explicit side is a real checker. If it is another LLM, results are weaker.

source: Sumers et al. (2023) Cognitive architectures for language agents (CoALA)
finding: Frames LLM agents with memory modules, action space and decision cycle from Soar-type architectures. Treats LLM weights as implicit procedural memory and code or prompts as explicit procedural memory.
numbers: No experiments. Survey of existing agents.
limits: A framework, not tested.
agent_relevance: Same implicit/explicit split used in this subfield. Our schema can be described in these terms.

source: Ustun et al. (2021) Controlling synthetic characters in simulations: a case for cognitive architectures and Sigma
finding: Sigma combines symbolic architectures, factor graphs and neural models under a graphical architecture hypothesis. Three proof of concept models are given.
numbers: No quantitative results in the text. Sigma uses a sum-product algorithm for all inference.
limits: Proof of concept only. Not compared against rivals.
agent_relevance: Sigma's one-mechanism design is elegant but untested at scale. Low value for us.

source: Chella, Frixione and Lieto (2018) Representational issues in the debate on the Standard Model of the Mind
finding: Critique: Soar, ACT-R and Sigma have limited, homogeneous knowledge bases and cannot handle typicality (prototype or exemplar) reasoning well. They suggest conceptual spaces.
numbers: No numbers. Names a size problem and a homogeneity problem.
limits: Position paper. Written before LLMs.
agent_relevance: LLMs now supply the large, varied knowledge. That was the main gap in hybrid architectures.

source: Trotter et al. (2020) Exploring variation between artificial grammar learning experiments: outlining a meta-analysis approach
finding: Meta-analysis of AGL, the classic implicit learning task. Learning is real and large overall, but publication bias was detected.
numbers: 66 articles, 78 studies, 3,559 subjects (156 effect sizes). Overall g=1.069, SE .130, 95% CI [.813, 1.326]. Peters' test for bias t(154)=-2.290, p=.023. Heterogeneity Q(155)=1185.657, p<.0001.
limits: Mixed human and animal studies. Does not test whether learning is implicit (unconscious). Search limited to auditory and visual.
agent_relevance: Implicit learning of structure is robust, but effect sizes are inflated by bias. Treat large claims with care.

source: Trotter et al. (2020) Exploring variation between artificial grammar learning experiments: outlining a meta-analysis approach
finding: Moderators of AGL: adults learn most, effect shrinks with more training trials, and repeated items at test inflate effects.
numbers: Human adults g=1.252 (CI .958-1.545); human children .615; non-human mammals .626; birds .428 (CI -.653 to 1.509, ns). Log training length b=-.188, p=.0006. Item repetition at test +1.051, p=.0002. Modality (visual vs auditory) not significant, p=.909.
limits: Training-length effect may reflect ceiling or design. Repetition is a design confound, not real structure learning.
agent_relevance: Part of the apparent implicit learning is surface cue use. Same worry for an LLM: pass on a test may be shallow patterns.

source: Leach and Weick (2018) Can people judge the veracity of their intuitions?
finding: People's trust in intuition did not predict how well they learned an artificial grammar. Confidence in the task tracked performance only weakly.
numbers: Meta-analysis of 3 own studies plus Pretz et al. (2010), N=400 and n=500 for the trust link. Trust vs learning r=-.05, 95% CI [-.17,.08], BF01=6.02. Nonsocial task r=-.20, n=178. Self-assessed vs actual performance r=.24, 95% CI [.14,.33].
limits: Student and online samples. Grammar task only. The weak confidence link is a limit, not proof of no metacognition.
agent_relevance: Implicit knowledge is poorly self-reported. Verbal confidence from a model should not be trusted as a switch between fast and slow.

source: Reber (1989) Implicit learning and tacit knowledge
finding: Source of the claim that implicitly learned content is richer than can be explained. Founding reference for the implicit side. Quoted via Sun (2025) only.
numbers: Not read. Quote seen in Sun (2025).
limits: Later critiques (Shanks and St John 1994; Newell and Shanks 2014) argue awareness tests are too insensitive. Not read this session.
agent_relevance: Do not assume implicit learning means no conscious knowledge.

source: Newell and Shanks (2014) Unconscious influences on decision making: a critical review
finding: Review argued that evidence for unconscious influences often fails because awareness measures are not exhaustive. Rival view to Reber-style claims.
numbers: Not read this session. No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened. Claim from memory; verify before use.
agent_relevance: Weakens the empirical base for the implicit half of dual-level models.

source: Sun, Slusarz and Terry (2005) Interaction of the explicit and implicit in skill learning: a dual-process approach, Psychological Review 112
finding: Main CLARION skill-learning paper. Reports synergy effects and simulations of process control, SRT and others.
numbers: Not read. Full text not found. Details taken only from the 2001 proceedings paper above.
limits: Full text unavailable; search budget used up.
agent_relevance: Priority to read for exact human numbers.
